which_results_affected: None. The Voronoi paper cites the FK paper once, in the Prior work subsection of the introduction, only to compare results. It says outright that the square-bond theorem is not used in its proof. Its main theorem and its corollaries (including cor:quenched-rectangles) do not depend on the FK paper. One sentence is affected: the prior-work remark that Cardy's formula 'is obtained' for square-lattice bond percolation, citing Theorem 1.2 of the FK paper. That is the FK paper's Cardy theorem, which the confirmed gap leaves unproven. So the sentence should say the result is claimed, not established. This is a wording fix and changes no proof.
evidence:
The citation appears once in the whole source. I grepped paper.tex, all nine files in sections/ and references.bib for the bib key, for 'OAI' and for 'bond', and for 'OpenAI' in references.bib. The only use is sections/00-introduction.tex lines 80-86 (Prior work subsection):
"The same Cardy function is obtained for critical square-lattice bond percolation under uniform marked-Jordan approximation \cite[Theorem~1.2]{OpenAISquareBond2026}. There the event is an actual open-edge path with all boundary edges sampled independently and no external connections; here it is an annealed closed-cell crossing in a fixed Jordan domain. The square-bond theorem is not used in our proof."
The bib entry (references.bib:236-243) is @misc{OpenAISquareBond2026, title = {Square-lattice FK interfaces and nested loops for $1\le q<4$}, ..., note = {Theorem~1.2}}.
Theorem 1.2 is the square-lattice bond (q=1) Cardy result. The confirmed gap in Sec. 7.3 (hol:disk leading to intro:main and the Cardy theorem) makes it unestablished, so the cited statement is itself one of the failed results. But it is used only as a comparison in the literature review. Nothing in sections 01-08 cites it or relies on it. The Voronoi paper's own proof uses its own color-switching observable in sections 01-08. Its probabilistic inputs come from other works: Tassion, AGMT, Vanneuville, Bollobás-Riordan and Smirnov.
